Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch

Repitch (speed and pitch together, like a record) or time-stretch (apart); semitones, percentages, and the sound of each.

A sample almost never arrives at the tempo and key of your track. There are two ways to change it.

Repitch: speed and pitch together

Play a record faster and it gets higher; slower and it gets lower. That is repitching. A turntable’s pitch fader does it, and so do the classic samplers (the E-mu SP-1200, the Akai MPC60, the SP-404’s pitch knob).

  • Twice as fast = one octave up (12 semitones). Half speed = an octave down.
  • One semitone is a speed change of about 5.95 % (the twelfth root of two is 1.0595).
  • So a turntable’s ±8 % pitch range is about ±1.3 semitones; ±16 % about ±2.6.

Repitching keeps transients sharp and sounds natural, because nothing is invented: it is the same sound, faster or slower. Pitching soul vocals up gave the “chipmunk soul” sound of early-2000s hip-hop; slowing whole songs down is the Houston “chopped and screwed” style.

Time-stretch: apart

Time-stretching changes the length without changing the pitch (and pitch-shifting the pitch without the length). The computer cuts the sound into tiny overlapping grains and spaces them further apart or closer together. Done simply, you hear it: drums smear, a “phasey” or metallic sound appears. Modern algorithms (Ableton Live’s Warp modes, élastique in many DAWs, DJ software’s key lock) hide it much better, but stretch anything far enough and it shows.

Hear the difference

  1. Pick pad 1 (a chord). Set Pitch to +5 in Repitch mode. Shorter and higher, like a sped-up record.
  2. Change Mode to Stretch. The same +5 semitones, but the chord keeps its length.
  3. Leave pitch at 0 and set Length to ×2 in each mode. Repitch: an octave down and twice as long. Stretch: same pitch, twice as long, and listen to the attack: blurred. This sampler uses plain overlap-add on purpose, so the smear is easy to hear.
  4. Load the Funky Break, slice At the hits, and stretch a snare to ×1.5 in each mode. Which would you put in a track?

Matching a sample to your track

The arithmetic: the speed you need is your tempo ÷ the sample’s tempo. A 90 BPM break in a 100 BPM track: 100 ÷ 90 = 1.111, so 11.1 % faster, which repitched is about +1.8 semitones. If the key matters, choose:

  • Repitch to the nearest key and adjust the track’s tempo to fit (producers often build the track at the sample’s speed), or
  • Stretch to the exact tempo and pitch-shift separately, accepting some artefacts.

The DJ’s version: pitch fader and key lock

On a turntable the pitch fader is repitch. Below, push deck A’s fader to +8 %: BPM and key both move; the readout shows the shift in semitones. DJ software and CDJs add key lock (Master Tempo on Pioneer gear): tempo changes, pitch stays, by time-stretching.

In other gear

Akai MPC Roland SP-404 Ableton Live
Repitch Tune (semitones, cents) Pitch knob / Speed Clip Transpose with Warp off, or Re-Pitch warp mode (Tempo and Warping)
Time-stretch Warp / Time Stretch Time Stretch (MKII: BPM sync) Warp modes: Beats, Tones, Texture, Complex
